terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run your file here to see the sorted lists and the stock answers.

tasks.title: Sort the names
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/sorting.js`, make `byName(scents)` return a new list of the scents from A to Z. `scents` stays as it was.

Check calls `byName` with lists of its own, one scent and none included, then makes sure the list it handed in has not changed and that a new list came back.
nextSteps: Read the lesson's part on what `sort` does to a list.
Make a copy of `scents`.
Sort the copy and give it back.
Run the file: the first line should start with Amber.
hints: `sort` puts a list in order, but it changes the list it is called on. The list you were handed belongs to someone else.
Copy first, with the spread form or `slice()`, then sort the copy. Text sorts from A to Z without anything more.

tasks.title: Cheapest first
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, make `cheapestFirst(prices)` return a new list of the prices from the lowest to the highest. `prices` stays as it was.

Check calls `cheapestFirst` with prices of its own, with different numbers of digits and two equal prices among them, then makes sure the list it handed in has not changed and that a new list came back. It also makes sure `cheapestFirst` uses `sort`.
nextSteps: Run the file once with a plain `sort` on a copy and look at the order.
Read the lesson's part on compare functions.
Give `sort` a compare function that puts the lower price first.
Sort a copy, give it back, and run the file again.
hints: Without help, `sort` compares items as text, so `'1100'` comes before `'900'` the way a dictionary would put them.
A compare function gets two items and gives back a number: below 0 when the first should come first, above 0 when the second should. Subtracting one price from the other gives exactly that.
The body is one line: `return [...prices].sort((a, b) => a - b)`.

tasks.title: The dearest few
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, make `dearest(prices, count)` return a new list of the `count` highest prices, the highest first. When `prices` has fewer than `count`, all of them come back, the highest first. `prices` stays as it was.

Check calls `dearest` with prices and counts of its own: equal prices, a count larger than the list, a count of 0 and an empty list included. It makes sure the list it handed in has not changed, that a new list came back, and that `dearest` uses `sort`.
nextSteps: Sort a copy of the prices so the highest comes first.
Keep the first `count` of them with the tool from the issue on copies.
Give that list back.
Run the file and try a count larger than the shelf.
hints: This is two jobs you know: sort a copy, then keep the start of it.
For the highest first, the compare function subtracts the other way round. `slice(0, count)` keeps the first `count` items and does not mind a list that is shorter.
The body is one line: `return [...prices].sort((a, b) => b - a).slice(0, count)`.

tasks.title: Time to pour?
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 4`, first write a function of your own, `isLow(count)`: it returns `true` when `count` is below 3, and `false` otherwise. It only helps `needsPouring`, so it stays off the export line.

Then make `needsPouring(stock)` return `true` when at least one count in `stock` is low, and `false` when none is. An empty list needs no pouring. Use `some` and `isLow`.

Check calls `isLow` with counts of its own, 3 included, then `needsPouring` with stock lists of its own, an empty one included. It makes sure `needsPouring` uses `some` and `isLow`.
nextSteps: Write `isLow` above `needsPouring`, from its name to its closing brace.
Read the lesson's part on `some` and `every`.
Hand `isLow` to `some` in `needsPouring` and give back its answer.
Run the file: today's stock has a low count.
hints: One list tool answers the question "is this true for at least one item?" with true or false.
`some` calls the function you give it with each item and stops at the first true. You can hand it `isLow` by its name, without round brackets.

tasks.title: Ready for the market
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 5`, make `readyForMarket(stock)` return `true` when every count in `stock` is 5 or more, and `false` when any is less. An empty list counts as ready: no scent is short. Use `every`.

Check calls `readyForMarket` with stock lists of its own: a count of exactly 5, a list with one short count, a list of one, and an empty list. It also makes sure `readyForMarket` uses `every`.
nextSteps: Write the question about one count: is it 5 or more?
Hand that question to `every`.
Give back what `every` answers.
Run the file and change a count in the demo to see the answer flip.
hints: `every` is the partner of `some`: true only when the question is true for every item.
5 or more includes 5 itself. `every` on an empty list gives back true, which is what the task asks for.
The body is one line: `return stock.every((count) => count >= 5)`.
